claims.text: CodePipeline's default execution mode is called `SUPERSEDED`.
CodePipeline's `SUPERSEDED` execution mode locks a stage to one execution at a time.
CodePipeline's `SUPERSEDED` execution mode only protects an execution once it's actually running.
In CodePipeline's `SUPERSEDED` execution mode, a newer execution can overtake an execution that is still waiting to enter a locked stage.
In CodePipeline's `SUPERSEDED` execution mode, an execution waiting to enter a locked stage can be dropped before it ever starts.

If a CodeBuild stage running `pulumi up` is busy and enough commits land, a queued execution waiting behind it can be superseded and never run, silently skipping a deployment rather than colliding with one already in progress.
Setting a CodePipeline pipeline's execution mode to `QUEUED` makes waiting executions form a queue so each one runs in turn rather than a later commit erasing an earlier one that never got its turn.
CodePipeline's `QUEUED` execution mode requires a V2 pipeline.
To use `QUEUED` execution mode, you must set both `executionMode` and `pipelineType` when defining the pipeline, using either the AWS CLI's `create-pipeline`/`update-pipeline` commands or as code.
The AWS CLI provides `create-pipeline` and `update-pipeline` commands that can be used to set a CodePipeline pipeline's `executionMode` and `pipelineType`.
The `aws.codepipeline.Pipeline` Pulumi resource has `executionMode` and `pipelineType` inputs.
Using Pulumi ESC to broker short-lived cloud credentials avoids storing provider keys as pipeline variables at all.
When two runs reach the same Pulumi stack at once, Pulumi Cloud grants the lease to only one of them.
When two runs reach the same Pulumi stack at once and Pulumi Cloud grants the lease to only one, the other run's `pulumi up` fails with an update conflict.
Azure Pipelines can prevent concurrent-run conflicts at the source with an exclusive lock check on the environment a deployment job targets.
In Azure Pipelines, the exclusive lock check is added from an environment's 'Approvals and checks' tab.
In Azure Pipelines, `lockBehavior` is a setting configured on the stage that references the environment's exclusive lock check.
Azure Pipelines YAML supports a stage-level `lockBehavior: sequential` property alongside a `Pulumi@1` task with `command: up`, `stack`, and `args` inputs.
In Azure Pipelines, `runLatest` is the default value of the `lockBehavior` setting.
With `lockBehavior: runLatest` in Azure Pipelines, only the most recently queued run ever acquires the lock.
With `lockBehavior: runLatest` in Azure Pipelines, an older run stuck waiting behind the lock is passed over rather than eventually applied.
`lockBehavior: runLatest` is acceptable for a preview environment where only the newest state matters.
`lockBehavior: runLatest` is not acceptable for a stack where every update needs to land.
With `lockBehavior: sequential` in Azure Pipelines, every queued stage runs against the lock in order, one at a time.
Pulumi Cloud itself serializes updates to a stack in the same one-at-a-time, in-order manner as Azure Pipelines' `lockBehavior: sequential`.
The Azure DevOps provider offers an `azuredevops.CheckExclusiveLock` resource for managing the exclusive lock check as code.
Azure DevOps itself — projects, repositories, pipelines, and service connections — can be managed as code with the Azure DevOps provider in the Pulumi Registry.
Pulumi offers native version control integrations for popular Git hosts, independent of TeamCity.
With a Pulumi version control integration configured, Pulumi Cloud posts infrastructure-change summaries as pull request comments.
With a Pulumi version control integration configured, Pulumi Cloud posts status checks as part of pull requests.
With a Pulumi version control integration configured, Pulumi Cloud links each stack update back to the commit and pull request that produced it.
If two runs of the same TeamCity build configuration reach the same Pulumi stack at once, Pulumi Cloud grants the update lease to only one of them.
When Pulumi Cloud grants the update lease to only one of two concurrent runs targeting the same stack, the other run's `pulumi up` fails with an update conflict.
TeamCity's own default behavior is to let build configurations run concurrently against as many free agents as it has available.
TeamCity's default concurrency behavior does nothing on its own to stop a race between two builds targeting the same Pulumi stack.
TeamCity build configurations have an advanced option called 'Limit the number of simultaneously running builds'.
The TeamCity 'Limit the number of simultaneously running builds' advanced option defaults to 0, meaning unlimited.
The TeamCity 'Limit the number of simultaneously running builds' advanced option is located under that build configuration's General Settings.
Setting the TeamCity 'Limit the number of simultaneously running builds' option to 1 causes a second build that would otherwise start immediately to be queued behind the first build instead.
When the TeamCity concurrency limit is set to 1, a queued second build runs only once the first build finishes.

Limiting TeamCity build concurrency to 1 produces the same one-at-a-time behavior that Pulumi Cloud's own per-stack lease provides, but applied earlier so the build never gets far enough to hit the conflict.
A clean TeamCity build agent starts with an empty plugin cache.
Because a clean build agent starts with an empty plugin cache, Pulumi re-downloads its provider plugins on every run.
Azure Pipelines supports adding an exclusive lock check to the environment a deployment job targets, to serialize deployments.
Azure Pipelines supports a `lockBehavior: sequential` setting on a stage.
AWS CodePipeline supports setting the pipeline's execution mode to `QUEUED` so waiting executions run in turn.
AWS CodePipeline's default execution mode lets a newer pipeline execution supersede an older one that is still waiting to start.
TeamCity supports a build configuration setting called "Limit the number of simultaneously running builds" that can be set to `1`.
